q: All waves are produced by a ____.
e: Wave generation always originates from a vibrating source that disturbs the surrounding medium.

q: Wave motion is a method of transferring ____ by successive disturbances through the medium.
e: Waves transfer energy from one location to another without the net movement of the medium itself.

q: This movement of energy takes place without transferring ____.
e: While energy propagates through the medium, the particles of the medium only vibrate about their equilibrium positions.

q: The mechanical waves need material medium to propagate and cannot pass through ____.
e: Mechanical waves, such as sound and seismic waves, require physical particles to transmit the disturbance.

q: Sound waves and seismic waves, which are produced by an earthquake, are ____.
e: These waves rely on a material medium for propagation, classifying them as mechanical waves.

q: Electromagnetic waves can pass through ____ and they do not need medium for propagation.
e: Unlike mechanical waves, electromagnetic waves can travel through empty space without a material medium.

q: Light wave and X-rays are ____.
e: Light and X-rays are examples of waves that do not require a medium and can travel through a vacuum.

q: Waves are classified as transverse and longitudinal waves depending on ____ of particles in the medium through which they propagate.
e: The classification of waves is based on the direction of particle vibration relative to the direction of wave propagation.

q: If the displacements of particles of the medium are ____ to the direction of the wave, such a wave is called a transverse wave.
e: In transverse waves, particle motion is at right angles to the direction the wave travels.

q: Waves in a vibrating string are ____.
e: The particles of a vibrating string move up and down while the wave travels horizontally, making them transverse.

q: Light waves and other electromagnetic waves are also ____.
e: Electromagnetic waves oscillate perpendicular to their direction of travel, classifying them as transverse.

q: If the displacements of particles of medium are ____ to the direction of the waves, such a wave is called a longitudinal wave.
e: In longitudinal waves, particle motion occurs in the same direction as the wave propagation.

q: Compressional waves in a slinky coiled spring and sound waves are ____.
e: These waves propagate through alternating regions of compression and rarefaction parallel to the direction of travel.

q: The highest and the lowest points which show the maximum displacement of vibrating particle from its rest position (or) equilibrium line are called ____ respectively.
e: The crest is the point of maximum positive displacement, while the trough is the point of maximum negative displacement.

q: The distance between any two consecutive wave crests (or) two consecutive wave troughs is called ____.
e: Wavelength is the spatial period of the wave, measured between two consecutive points in the same phase.

q: The unit of wavelength in SI unit is ____.
e: As a measure of distance, the standard SI unit for wavelength is the metre.

q: Generally the wavelength is the distance between two nearest points of ____.
e: Points in the same phase have identical displacement and velocity at any given instant.

q: The number of complete waves passing a point per second of a vibrating source is also called ____.
e: Frequency measures how often the wave cycle repeats per unit of time.

q: The SI unit of frequency is ____.
e: One hertz is defined as one complete wave cycle per second.

q: One hertz is equal to ____.
e: This is the fundamental definition of the hertz unit in wave mechanics.

q: The time taken by the wave to travel the distance between any two consecutive wave crests (or) the time required for one complete vibration is called ____ of a wave.
e: The period is the temporal duration of one full wave cycle.

q: The unit of period is the ____.
e: Time intervals in wave motion, such as the period, are measured in seconds in the SI system.

q: The period is the ____ of the frequency.
e: Mathematically, the period $T$ and frequency $f$ are related by the equation $T = 1/f$.

q: The amplitude of a wave is the ____ of displacement of vibrating particle.
e: Amplitude represents the greatest distance a particle moves from its equilibrium position.

q: Velocity of wave is the ____ with which a wave crest travels.
e: Wave velocity describes how fast the wave profile propagates through the medium.

q: The unit of wave velocity is ____.
e: As a measure of speed, wave velocity is expressed in metres per second in the SI system.

q: Most of the periodic waves are represented by ____ graphs.
e: Periodic wave motion is mathematically modeled using sinusoidal functions.

q: The relationship between the frequency, wavelength and velocity of a periodic wave can be obtained by ____.
e: This fundamental wave equation states that wave velocity equals the product of frequency and wavelength.

q: A displacement-distance graph describes the displacement of all particles at a ____.
e: This graph provides a snapshot of the wave's shape across space at a single moment.

q: Note that displacement of particle is plotted on ____ and distance moved by the wave is on x-axis.
e: In a displacement-distance graph, the vertical axis represents particle displacement.

q: A displacement-time graph describes the displacement of particle of a certain position as a ____ taken to travel by a wave.
e: This graph tracks how the displacement of a single particle changes over time.

q: The surface that joins all the points of same phase is called ____.
e: A wavefront represents the continuous locus of points that are oscillating in unison.

q: When a series of wave strike an obstacle, they are ____.
e: This reversal of direction upon hitting a boundary is the fundamental nature of wave reflection.

q: This turning back of waves is called ____.
e: Reflection occurs when waves bounce off a barrier or obstacle.

q: When waves strike a ____, the waves are reflected from the barrier.
e: A straight barrier produces a predictable reflection where the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

q: The angle of incidence is equal to the ____.
e: This is the law of reflection, which applies to all types of waves.

q: The wavelength and velocity of the wave remain ____ in reflection of wave.
e: Since the medium does not change during reflection, the wave's speed and wavelength are unaffected.

q: The speed of water waves depends on the ____.
e: Water wave velocity is directly influenced by the depth of the medium through which it travels.

q: It ____ when the depth of water becomes less deep.
e: Shallower water offers more resistance, causing the wave speed to drop.

q: When water waves pass from deep to shallow water the velocity of wave is ____ and the wavelength is shorter or vice-versa.
e: As velocity decreases in shallow water, the wavelength must also decrease to maintain a constant frequency.

q: When waves are incident to the boundary with an angle, the ____ of the waves changes.
e: A change in wave speed at a boundary causes the wave to bend, altering its direction of travel.

q: Such a change in direction is called ____.
e: Refraction is the bending of waves as they pass from one medium or depth to another.

q: It can be noticed that in refraction, the wavelength and velocity change but ____ remains the same.
e: Frequency is determined by the source and does not change when a wave enters a new medium.

q: Diffraction is the ____ from the straight-on direction through a gap (or) moves around an obstacle.
e: Diffraction describes how waves bend and spread out after passing through an opening or around a barrier.

q: The wave that passes the edges of the gap of the obstacle ____.
e: This spreading is the defining characteristic of wave diffraction.

q: The wider the gap, the ____ the waves spread out.
e: Diffraction is most pronounced when the gap size is comparable to the wavelength; a wider gap reduces this effect.

q: The narrower the gap, the ____ the waves spread out.
e: A narrower gap causes a greater degree of wave spreading due to increased diffraction.

q: Sound is a form of ____ that is transferred from one place to another in a certain medium.
e: Sound is mechanical energy transmitted through a medium via particle vibrations.

q: Sound wave is produced by a ____ placed in a medium.
e: The initial disturbance that creates a sound wave is always a vibrating source.

q: The pressure changes occur ____ in the medium by vibrating object.
e: Sound propagation involves alternating regions of high pressure (compression) and low pressure (rarefaction).

q: Sound wave propagates as a series of ____ like longitudinal waves on a vibrating spring.
e: These alternating pressure regions are the mechanism by which longitudinal sound waves travel.

q: Unlike electromagnetic waves, sound waves need a ____ to propagate.
e: Sound is a mechanical wave and cannot exist or travel without material particles to transmit the vibration.

q: Sound wave cannot travel through ____.
e: The absence of particles in a vacuum prevents the transmission of sound energy.

q: The compression is created in the medium as the vibrating object ____.
e: Forward motion of the vibrating source forces adjacent particles closer, increasing local pressure.

q: The compression region has ____.
e: Compression is defined by an increase in molecular density and pressure within the medium.

q: When the object moves back, the molecules are spread out and ____ is created and the pressure of that region is low.
e: Rarefaction is the region of low pressure and density that follows a compression in a sound wave.

q: The average person can only hear sound that has a frequency higher than ____ and lower than $20\,000 \text{ Hz}$.
e: The lower limit of the human audible range is typically 20 hertz.

q: This interval of frequency is called the ____ (or) hearing range.
e: The audible range defines the spectrum of sound frequencies detectable by the human ear.

q: Sound waves with frequencies greater than $20\,000 \text{ Hz}$ are called ____.
e: Ultrasound refers to sound frequencies that are too high for human hearing.

q: Some objects vibrating with frequencies under $20 \text{ Hz}$ produces sound which cannot be heard by ____.
e: Frequencies below the human hearing threshold are inaudible to people but may be detected by other animals.

q: This is called ____.
e: Infrasound refers to sound waves with frequencies below 20 Hz.

q: Generally, the speed of sound depends on the ____ of the medium.
e: The physical properties of the medium, particularly its density and elasticity, determine how fast sound travels.

q: The denser the medium is, the ____ the speed because the particles of the medium are tightly bound together.
e: In denser media, particles are closer together, allowing the vibrational disturbance to be transferred more rapidly.

q: At $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ the speed of sound in air is ____.
e: This is the standard reference speed of sound in air at freezing temperature.

q: Whenever the air temperature increases by $1^{\circ}\text{C}$, speed of sound will increase by ____.
e: Sound travels faster in warmer air because the molecules have more kinetic energy to transmit the wave.

q: The speed of sound in air can be expressed as ____.
e: This formula calculates the speed of sound in air based on the absolute temperature $T$ in Kelvin.

q: Here $T$ is given in ____ and $v$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
e: The temperature variable in the exact speed of sound formula must be in absolute Kelvin.

q: The above relation can be approximated by ____.
e: This linear approximation is often used for quick calculations of sound speed at different Celsius temperatures.

q: In air medium, the speed of sound increases by ____ with temperature rise by one degree ($1^{\circ}\text{C}$ or $1\text{K}$).
e: For every degree Celsius increase in temperature, the speed of sound in air increases by approximately 0.6 metres per second.
